guide.title: Unit 7: Global Conflict: review guide
guide.intro: The twentieth century opened with old empires collapsing and new powers rising. Two world wars, a global depression, and the rise of authoritarian states followed, and governments committed mass atrocities on an unprecedented scale. This unit covers causes, the conduct of total war, and the consequences.

sections.title: Shifting power and World War I
body: Old land empires weakened or fell: the Qing dynasty ended in 1911, revolution began in Mexico in 1910, and the Russian, Ottoman, and Austro-Hungarian empires collapsed during or after World War I. Causes of the war included imperial rivalry, militarism, alliance systems, and nationalism; the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set it off.

World War I was a total war: governments mobilized whole economies, used propaganda, and recruited soldiers from colonies. On the Western Front, machine guns, artillery, and poison gas produced trench warfare and enormous casualties.
points: Separate long-term causes from the immediate trigger.
Total war blurred the line between soldiers and civilians.

sections.title: The interwar period
body: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany for the war and imposed reparations. The League of Nations was created, but the United States never joined. Former Ottoman lands became League mandates under British and French control.

The Great Depression began in 1929 and spread worldwide. Responses varied: the U.S. New Deal expanded government's role in the economy; the Soviet Union pursued state-run Five-Year Plans and forced collectivization; and fascist and militarist regimes in Italy, Germany, and Japan promised national revival through authoritarian rule and expansion.
points: Connect economic crisis to political change.
Unresolved tensions after 1919 helped cause World War II.

sections.title: World War II and mass atrocities
body: Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and China (1937); Germany expanded in Europe and invaded Poland in 1939. Appeasement failed. The war was fought with mass mobilization, including women in industry and millions of colonial soldiers, and with bombing of cities, ending with the U.S. atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

The century saw repeated mass atrocities: the Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire (1915), the Holodomor famine in Soviet Ukraine (1932–1933), the Holocaust in which Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jews and millions of others, and later the Cambodian genocide (1975–1979) and the Rwandan genocide (1994).
points: Causation questions ask how ideology, war, and state power combined.
Compare atrocities by perpetrator, target group, and context.

example.prompt: Explain one way the Great Depression contributed to the outbreak of World War II.
example.solution: Mass unemployment and economic collapse discredited democratic governments in countries such as Germany, helping the Nazis take power in 1933; their expansionist goals, along with Japanese expansion in Asia, led to war.

misconceptions: “World War I was caused only by an assassination.”
The assassination was a trigger; alliances, militarism, imperialism, and nationalism were deeper causes.
“The Great Depression affected only the United States.”
It spread worldwide through trade and finance.
“Mass atrocities happened only in World War II.”
Genocides and state-made famines occurred throughout the century.
“Colonies played no role in the world wars.”
Millions of colonial soldiers and workers served the imperial powers.

passages.title: Source A: Siegfried Sassoon, “Counter-Attack,” 1918
text: “We’d gained our first objective hours before / While dawn broke like a face with blinking eyes, / Pallid, unshaven and thirsty, blind with smoke. / Things seemed all right at first. We held their line, / With bombers posted, Lewis guns well placed, / And clink of shovels deepening the shallow trench. . . . / He crouched and flinched, dizzy with galloping fear, / Sick for escape,—loathing the strangled horror / And butchered, frantic gestures of the dead. . . . / Down, and down, and down, he sank and drowned, / Bleeding to death. The counter-attack had failed.”
passages.attribution: Siegfried Sassoon, a British officer and poet who served on the Western Front, from a poem published in 1918. (Lewis guns were light machine guns.) Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2, section 11.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (written in English and published in 1918). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2 (openstax.org/books/world-history-volume-2/pages/11-3-total-war); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of the interwar years, 1919–1939
text: “The peace of 1919 satisfied almost no one. The Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame for the war and to pay reparations, and many Germans called it a dictated peace. The new League of Nations lacked the United States. Arab lands taken from the Ottoman Empire became League mandates governed by Britain and France, not the independent states many Arabs had been promised. Then, after 1929, the Great Depression spread around the world. The United States answered with the New Deal, which expanded the government's role in the economy, while the Soviet Union pushed ahead with state-run Five-Year Plans. In Germany, Italy, and Japan, leaders promising order and national glory gained power.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of World War II as total war
text: “World War II mobilized societies more completely than any war before it. Factories in the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union turned out tanks and aircraft by the tens of thousands, and millions of women took industrial jobs. Britain drew more than two million soldiers from India, and France recruited heavily in Africa. Civilians became targets on a vast scale: German, British, American, and Japanese bombers struck cities, and in August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. In occupied Europe, Nazi Germany carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, and others it deemed undesirable.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of collapsing empires and mass atrocities
text: “Within a few years after 1910 several old empires fell. The Qing dynasty ended in 1911, and World War I destroyed the Russian, Ottoman, and Austro-Hungarian empires. Upheaval of this kind repeatedly opened the way to mass violence. During the war, Ottoman authorities deported and killed hundreds of thousands of Armenians. In 1932 and 1933, Stalin's forced collectivization and grain seizures caused a famine in Soviet Ukraine, the Holodomor, that killed millions. Later in the century, the Khmer Rouge killed some two million Cambodians between 1975 and 1979, and in 1994 Hutu extremists in Rwanda murdered hundreds of thousands of Tutsi in about a hundred days.”

questions.prompt: Details such as “the shallow trench” and “Lewis guns well placed” show that Source A describes
choices: a naval battle in the North Sea
trench warfare on the Western Front
a cavalry charge in the Russian steppe
guerrilla fighting in a colonial jungle
questions.explanation: The trench, the line, and the machine guns place the poem in the trench warfare of the Western Front, where Sassoon served.
choiceExplanations: The poem describes trenches, not ships.
No horses or cavalry appear.
The setting is a fixed line of trenches, not guerrilla war.

He is killed, and the counter-attack fails.
He leads his unit to capture the enemy line.
He escapes the battle and returns home safely.
questions.explanation: He sinks down, “Bleeding to death. The counter-attack had failed.”
choiceExplanations: Nothing suggests a promotion.
The attack fails.
He dies on the battlefield.

questions.prompt: The poem's picture of combat most directly contrasts with
choices: Sassoon's own experience as an officer at the front
accounts showing heavy casualties on the Western Front
propaganda presenting the war as glorious
the idea that soldiers felt fear in battle
questions.explanation: Sassoon's images of fear, mud, and pointless death challenged official images of a heroic war.
choiceExplanations: The poem draws on his experience; it does not contrast with it.
The poem agrees with accounts of heavy casualties.
The poem itself shows the soldier's fear.

questions.prompt: Which feature of World War I does the poem best illustrate?
choices: The use of atomic weapons against cities
Industrial weapons producing stalemate and mass death
Rapid advances that ended the war within weeks
A war fought mainly by volunteers from neutral countries
questions.explanation: Machine guns (the Lewis guns) and the failed counter-attack in which a soldier bleeds to death in the mud reflect the costly, deadlocked fighting of the Western Front.
choiceExplanations: Atomic weapons were first used in 1945.
The war lasted more than four years.
The armies were national and imperial forces.

lands returned to Ottoman rule

choices: German resentment of the Versailles treaty
The New Deal's expansion of government
The creation of state-run Soviet factories
The Arab support for British mandates
questions.explanation: Many Germans saw the treaty as unjust, a grievance that the Nazis exploited in pursuing expansion.
choiceExplanations: The New Deal was a domestic economic program.
Soviet planning was a response to economic goals, not a direct cause of the war.
The source says many Arabs had been promised independence instead.

questions.prompt: How did the U.S. and Soviet responses to economic crisis in Source B differ?
choices: Neither country changed its economic policies in the 1930s.
The United States rejected any government role in the economy, while the Soviets favored free markets.
The New Deal kept a market economy, while Soviet planning was fully state-run.
Both ended private property and created a command economy.
questions.explanation: The New Deal expanded government within a market system; the Soviet Five-Year Plans placed industry entirely under the state.
choiceExplanations: Both countries changed course in the 1930s.
The New Deal expanded the government's role, and the Soviets rejected free markets.
The United States kept private property.

choices: only professional soldiers took part in the fighting
civilians were protected from all attacks
the war was limited to a single continent
whole societies and economies were mobilized for it
questions.explanation: Factories, women workers, colonial soldiers, and attacks on cities show the mobilization of entire societies.
choiceExplanations: Millions of civilians and colonial soldiers took part.
The source says civilians “became targets on a vast scale.”
It was fought in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Nazi Germany's systematic murder of about six million Jews
the recruitment of soldiers from India
the bombing of British cities by German aircraft during the war
questions.explanation: The source defines it as “the systematic murder of about six million Jews,” along with other targeted groups.
choiceExplanations: The atomic bombs are a separate event.
Colonial recruitment is a separate development.
Bombing of cities is a separate development.

an end to European rule within a year
the colonies joining the Axis powers

The colonies supported the Allied empires.

it involved no economic mobilization
it was fought without colonial soldiers
questions.explanation: Mass bombing of cities, atomic weapons, and the Holocaust made civilian deaths far greater than in World War I.
choiceExplanations: Machine guns were central in World War I.
The source describes vast economic mobilization.

questions.prompt: The atrocities against Armenians, Cambodians, and Tutsi described in Source D share which feature?
choices: All were carried out by the same government
All resulted from natural disasters
All took place before World War I began
Groups were targeted amid war or upheaval.
questions.explanation: Each took place amid war or revolution, and each targeted a group defined by its ethnicity, religion, or politics.
choiceExplanations: They were carried out by different regimes.
They were human-made atrocities.
They took place in 1915, 1975–1979, and 1994.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the pattern described in Source D?
choices: Mass atrocities happened only where governments had collapsed entirely.
Only colonial powers carried out mass atrocities in the twentieth century.
States in crisis used ideology to blame and destroy targeted groups.
Atrocities ended once the world wars were over.
questions.explanation: Regimes facing war or revolution, from the Ottoman government to the Khmer Rouge, defined certain groups as enemies and targeted them.
choiceExplanations: Strong states, such as the Soviet Union, also carried out atrocities.
The examples include non-colonial regimes.
The source gives examples from 1975 and 1994.
